Title: Is one better than another?: A randomized clinical trial of manual therapy for patients with chronic neck pain.

Journal/Date: Manual therapy (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Adult, Aged, Analysis of Variance, Chronic Pain, Disability Evaluation, Double-Blind Method, Exercise Therapy, Female


--- ABSTRACT ---
Our purpose was to compare the effectiveness of three manual therapy techniques: high velocity, low amplitude (HVLA), mobilization (Mob) and sustained natural apophyseal glide (SNAG) in patients with chronic neck pain (CNP). The randomized controlled trial included patients with mechanically reproducible CNP, who were randomized to the treatment group. Outcome measures were the Visual Analogue scale (VAS), Neck Disability Index (NDI), Global Rating of Change (GROC) and Cervical Range of Motion (CROM). Two-way repeated measures analysis of variance compared outcomes at baseline, at the end of treatment and 1, 2 and 3 months after treatment. A total of 51 subjects completed the trial. No significant differences were found between HVLA, Mob and SNAG at the end of treatment and during the follow-up in any of the analysed outcomes. There were no differences in satisfaction for all techniques. The results lead to the conclusion that there is no long-term difference between the application of HVLA, Mob and SNAG in pain, disability and cervical range of motion for patients with CNP.

Title: The Effectiveness of Mulligan's Techniques in Non-Specific Neck Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

Journal/Date: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy (2025)

MeSH Keywords: Humans, Neck Pain, Physical Therapy Modalities, Range of Motion, Articular, Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic, Treatment Outcome


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE]: Mulligan's techniques, such as Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glides (SNAGs) and Natural Apophyseal Glides (NAGs), are commonly applied by physiotherapists when treating patients with non-specific neck pain (NP). However, there has been no comprehensive synthesis of their effects in NP. This review aimed to assess the effectiveness of Mulligan's techniques in reducing pain, improving disability, and enhancing cervical range of motion (CROM) in adults with acute, subacute, or chronic NP.
[METHODS]: A systematic review with meta-analysis was conducted on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing Mulligan's techniques with other interventions in adults with NP. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias (RoB) assessment. Meta-analyses were performed when clinical homogeneity was present; otherwise, a narrative synthesis was used. Certainty of evidence was rated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) approach.
[RESULTS]: Thirty-three studies were included. For acute and mixed (acute/subacute/chronic) NP, Mulligan's techniques were no more effective than other interventions for pain reduction, disability improvement, or CROM enhancement. However, in patients with chronic or uncertain chronicity NP, SNAGs combined with other interventions demonstrated superior outcomes-both statistically and sometimes clinically-compared to certain treatments like exercises and muscle-energy techniques, for reducing pain and disability and improving CROM. The certainty of evidence was rated very low.
[DISCUSSION]: Mulligan's techniques appear to be safe, simple, and potentially beneficial for managing mixed or chronic NP when combined with other interventions, presenting results that may be comparable or occasionally superior to other standard techniques.
[IMPLICATIONS FOR PHYSIOTHERAPY PRACTICE]: Physiotherapists may consider incorporating Mulligan's techniques, especially SNAGs, within broader NP treatment strategies, as they offer a feasible, low-risk option for improving patient outcomes, particularly for chronic NP cases when used alongside other therapies.

=== PMID: 24792139 ===

Title: Effects of cervical spine manual therapy on range of motion, head repositioning, and balance in participants with cervicogenic dizziness: a randomized controlled trial.

Journal/Date: Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Adolescent, Adult, Aged, Aged, 80 and over, Cervical Vertebrae, Chronic Disease, Dizziness, Double-Blind Method


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: To evaluate and compare the effects of 2 manual therapy interventions on cervical spine range of motion (ROM), head repositioning accuracy, and balance in patients with chronic cervicogenic dizziness.
[DESIGN]: Randomized controlled trial with 12-week follow-up using blinded outcome assessment.
[SETTING]: University School of Health Sciences.
[PARTICIPANTS]: Participants (N=86; mean age ± SD, 62.0 ± 12.7 y; 50% women) with chronic cervicogenic dizziness.
[INTERVENTIONS]: Participants were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 groups: sustained natural apophyseal glides (SNAGs) with self-SNAG exercises, passive joint mobilization (PJM) with ROM exercises, or a placebo. Participants each received 2 to 6 treatments over 6 weeks.
[MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES]: Cervical ROM, head repositioning accuracy, and balance.
[RESULTS]: SNAG therapy resulted in improved (P ≤.05) cervical spine ROM in all 6 physiological cervical spine movement directions immediately posttreatment and at 12 weeks. Treatment with PJM resulted in improvement in 1 of the 6 cervical movement directions posttreatment and 1 movement direction at 12 weeks. There was a greater improvement (P<.01) after SNAGs than PJM in extension (mean difference, -7.5°; 95% confidence interval [CI], -13° to -2.0°) and right rotation (mean difference, -6.8°; 95% CI, -11.5° to -2.1°) posttreatment. Manual therapy had no effect on balance or head repositioning accuracy.
[CONCLUSIONS]: SNAG treatment improved cervical ROM, and the effects were maintained for 12 weeks after treatment. PJM had very limited impact on cervical ROM. There was no conclusive effect of SNAGs or PJMs on joint repositioning accuracy or balance in people with cervicogenic dizziness.

key_findings.finding: Direct evidence for the requested comparison is one randomized controlled trial (PMID 25097535; Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences, 2014) in 102 adults with non-specific neck pain: 6 weeks of SNAGs plus isometric exercise training (n=51) produced greater between-group improvement than SNAGs alone (n=51) for pain (VAS between-group p=0.013) and disability (NDI between-group p=0.003). Within-group reporting showed SNAG+isometric: VAS 7→4 and NDI 40→15; SNAG alone: VAS 7→4 and NDI 42→30. The abstract does not report cervical ROM, adverse events, or longer-term follow-up.

source_tools.relevance: Direct full abstract and results preview for the SNAG-versus-SNAG+isometric randomized trial

key_findings.finding: The direct trial supports an added disability benefit from isometric exercise, but the pain result is difficult to interpret clinically because both groups improved by the same reported absolute VAS amount (7 to 4), despite a statistically significant between-group test; the report also inconsistently describes intervention duration as 6 weeks in the abstract/results versus four weeks in one results sentence. These reporting issues, lack of ROM data, no follow-up, and limited methodological detail in the abstract reduce confidence in the estimate.

source_tools.relevance: Directly reported numerical outcomes and duration inconsistency in the primary trial

key_findings.finding: A separate randomized clinical trial in 51 completers with mechanically reproducible chronic neck pain compared SNAGs with HVLA and mobilization, measuring VAS, NDI, global rating of change, and cervical ROM. It found no significant between-group differences at treatment completion or 1–3 month follow-up for any outcome; thus SNAGs were not superior to the other manual-therapy comparators, although this study did not test isometric exercise augmentation (PMID 24467843; Manual Therapy, 2014).

source_tools.relevance: Direct abstract of comparative SNAG manual-therapy RCT

key_findings.finding: The 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis of 33 RCTs in adults with non-specific neck pain concluded that Mulligan techniques were generally not superior for acute or mixed-duration neck pain, whereas SNAGs combined with other interventions sometimes outperformed exercise or muscle-energy comparators for chronic or unclear-duration neck pain on pain, disability, and CROM; certainty of evidence was very low. This is directionally consistent with a possible benefit from adding exercise, but it does not establish that isometric training specifically is superior to SNAGs alone.

source_tools.relevance: Systematic-review abstract and results preview synthesizing the broader RCT evidence

key_findings.finding: A related RCT in chronic cervicogenic dizziness (not non-specific neck pain) found SNAGs plus self-SNAG exercises improved all six cervical ROM directions and produced greater post-treatment gains than passive mobilization in extension (mean difference −7.5°, 95% CI −13 to −2) and right rotation (−6.8°, 95% CI −11.5 to −2.1), with effects maintained at 12 weeks; it should be considered indirect evidence and not pooled with the target population (PMID 24792139; Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2014).
